(CNN) — They included parents and children, business magnates and religious figures, people from the West and from Asia, all drawn to Mumbai for separate purposes. Yet this week, they were caught in the same deadly wave of bullets and blasts during a series of terrorist attacks across the Indian metropolis.

Kia Scherr, shown at left, told CNN that her husband, Alan Scherr, and their daughter, Naomi, died in Mumbai.

At least 183 people were killed in the attacks, which struck several busy landmarks around the city, including places often visited by tourists. The deaths have devastated families and communities, while many victims still have not been officially identified. Early details about some of those killed have begun to surface, most of them involving foreign nationals. Information about Indian victims has been more limited.

The U.S. State Department said Friday that five Americans had been confirmed dead, including a father and daughter from a meditation group in Virginia.

Kia Scherr told CNN on Friday that her husband, Alan, 58, and daughter, Naomi, 13, were among those killed. She said she knew they had been eating at the Oberoi hotel in Mumbai when shooting erupted Wednesday night. According to Scherr, her final conversation with them was on Thursday.

Friends described the Scherrs’ trip to Mumbai.

Scherr said her husband and daughter had arrived in India on November 17 and were scheduled to depart on Monday. A spokeswoman for The Synchronicity Foundation, a meditation organization located near Charlottesville, Virginia, said Alan and Naomi were part of a 25-member group visiting India. The foundation’s website said the other Synchronicity members who had been staying at the Oberoi had all been located and were safe.

Hemant Karkare, the head of Maharashtra state’s Anti-Terrorism Squad, was one of at least 16 Indian law enforcement personnel killed during the attacks. Mumbai is located in Maharashtra. According to CNN’s sister network CNN-IBN, Karkare was leading an operation against the gunmen late Wednesday when he was shot three times in the chest.

CNN-IBN reported that Karkare joined the Indian Police Service in 1982 and became chief of the ATS in January after serving seven years in Austria with the Research and Analysis Wing, India’s external intelligence agency.

Five hostages, among them a rabbi and his wife, were killed during a siege at Chabad House, according to Rabbi Zalman Shmotkin, a spokesman in the United States for Chabad-Lubavitch International.

Rabbi Gavriel Noach Holtzberg, the community’s envoy in Mumbai, and his wife, Rivka, had been taken hostage inside Chabad House, which is also known in Mumbai as Nariman House. The site serves as the Mumbai headquarters for the Chabad community, a Hasidic Jewish movement.

Gavriel Holtzberg, 29, was born in Israel and moved with his parents to Brooklyn, New York, when he was 9. Rivka Holtzberg, 28, was from Afula, Israel, the organization said.

Chabad-Lubavitch International said the Holtzbergs came to Mumbai in 2003 to support and serve the city’s Jewish community.

“As emissaries to Mumbai, Gabi and Rivky gave up the comforts of the West in order to spread Jewish pride in a corner of the world that was a frequent stop for throngs of Israeli tourists,” Rabbi Moshe Kotlarsky, vice chairman of Merkos L’Inyonei Chinuch, the educational branch of Chabad-Lubavitch, said in a statement.

The organization said Gavriel Holtzberg called the Israeli Consulate to report that armed men were inside his home. “In the middle of the conversation, the line went dead,” the organization said. It did not specify when the call occurred.

Haaretz, an Israeli newspaper, reported that a cook at the center, after barricading herself in a room, took the couple’s son and escaped with another person. Rabbi Yehuda Krinsky, chairman of the educational and social services arms of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement, said the boy’s second birthday was Saturday.

“Today, he became an orphan,” Krinsky said during a news conference in New York. Krinsky also pledged that the Chabad community would raise the child.

The couple’s other child was not in Mumbai when the attacks took place and is safe, Krinsky said.

Others were also confirmed dead.

CNN’s Zain Verjee and Emanuella Grinberg contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**Mumbai terror attacks: Remembering the foreigners and Indian heroes among the victims**

**MUMBAI, India** — The 2008 Mumbai terror attacks left a city in flames, a nation in mourning and families around the world grieving loved ones who had traveled to India for work, faith, business or vacation — and never came home.

Over nearly three days, gunmen attacked luxury hotels, a train station, a Jewish community center, a café and other locations across India’s financial capital. By the time the siege ended, 166 people had been killed and hundreds more injured.

Among the dead were Indians from all walks of life — hotel workers, police officers, commuters and bystanders — as well as foreign nationals from several countries, including the United States, Israel, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, Canada and Australia.

For many outside India, the names Alan and Naomi Scherr, Rabbi Gavriel and Rivka Holtzberg, and Hemant Karkare came to symbolize the human cost of the attacks: a father and daughter on a spiritual trip, a young Jewish couple serving a small community, and a senior Indian police officer who ran toward danger.

### A father and daughter killed while visiting Mumbai

Alan Scherr, 58, and his 13-year-old daughter, Naomi, were Americans from Virginia who had traveled to India with a meditation group. They were killed at the Oberoi-Trident hotel complex, one of the major targets of the attacks.

Friends and family remembered Naomi as bright, joyful and deeply compassionate. Alan was described as a devoted father and longtime spiritual seeker.

Their deaths resonated widely in the United States, not only because of Naomi’s young age, but because of the way their family later spoke publicly about forgiveness in the face of devastating loss.

### A Jewish center becomes a target

At Nariman House, also known as the Chabad House, Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg and his wife, Rivka, were killed after gunmen stormed the Jewish outreach center they ran in Mumbai.

The Holtzbergs, originally from Israel, had moved to India as emissaries of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. They offered a place of worship, meals and community for Jewish residents and travelers in the city.

Their 2-year-old son, Moshe, survived after being rescued by his Indian nanny, Sandra Samuel, who carried him to safety during the attack. Images of the child’s rescue became one of the most haunting and widely remembered stories of the siege.

The killings at Nariman House underscored the international nature of the attacks and the targeting of Jews far from Israel.

### Hemant Karkare: An officer remembered for courage

Hemant Karkare, the chief of Mumbai’s Anti-Terrorism Squad, was among the senior police officials killed while responding to the attacks.

Karkare was not a foreign victim, but his death became central to India’s memory of the assault. He was killed along with other officers as they pursued the attackers in the early hours of the crisis.

A respected investigator, Karkare was later honored posthumously with the Ashoka Chakra, one of India’s highest peacetime gallantry awards.

His death highlighted the sacrifice of Mumbai police officers, many of whom confronted heavily armed attackers with limited protection and little time to assess the scale of the assault.

### A global tragedy in one city

The attackers targeted places that reflected Mumbai’s international identity: the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident, Leopold Café, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus railway station and Nariman House.

Foreign victims included business travelers, tourists, aid workers and religious visitors. Some had been in India for only a short time. Others had built lives and communities there.

The attacks were later blamed on the Pakistan-based militant group Lashkar-e-Taiba. Only one gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was captured alive. He was tried, convicted and executed in India in 2012.

More than 15 years later, the victims are remembered not only by nationality or circumstance, but by the lives they lived: a teenage girl traveling with her father, a rabbi and his wife welcoming strangers, police officers who answered the call, hotel staff who helped guests escape, and ordinary people caught in an extraordinary act of terror.

For Mumbai, the scars remain. So do the stories of those who were lost.

**BREAKING NEWS: Aftermath of the Mumbai Terror Attacks**

**Mumbai, India** — Indian authorities are continuing to assess the devastation left by the coordinated terror attacks that struck Mumbai over three days, targeting hotels, a train station, a Jewish community center, a café and other sites across India’s financial capital.

Officials have confirmed that **166 people were killed** and **more than 300 others injured** in the attacks, which began on November 26, 2008. The victims included Indian citizens, foreign nationals, hotel staff, security personnel and members of the Jewish community.

Among those killed were **six Americans**, according to U.S. officials. American victims included visitors and residents caught in the attacks at multiple locations, including the **Oberoi-Trident hotel** and **Nariman House**, also known as the **Chabad House**, a Jewish outreach center.

Indian security forces also suffered significant losses. Several police officers were killed in the initial response, including senior Mumbai police officials **Hemant Karkare**, the chief of the Anti-Terrorism Squad; **Ashok Kamte**, an additional police commissioner; and encounter specialist **Vijay Salaskar**. Indian commandos were later deployed to retake the besieged sites, and members of the National Security Guard were also killed during the operations.

One of the most harrowing standoffs unfolded at **Chabad House**, where gunmen took hostages inside the building. After a prolonged siege, Indian commandos stormed the center. Authorities later confirmed that several hostages inside had been killed, including **Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg** and his wife, **Rivka Holtzberg**, who ran the center. Their young son, **Moshe**, survived after being carried to safety by his nanny, **Sandra Samuel**, in a rescue that drew international attention.

The attacks were carried out by 10 gunmen who arrived by sea and struck multiple targets across Mumbai. Indian officials attributed the assault to the Pakistan-based militant group **Lashkar-e-Taiba**. One attacker, **Ajmal Kasab**, was captured alive, while the others were killed during security operations.

The aftermath has prompted a sweeping investigation, heightened security across India, and renewed tensions between India and Pakistan. International leaders have condemned the attacks, calling them one of the deadliest acts of terrorism in India’s modern history.

(CNN) -- They were fathers and daughters, tycoons and spiritualists, travelers and hotel workers, students and executives — people from India and around the world whose lives converged in Mumbai and ended in a coordinated terrorist assault that stunned the city and the globe.

Over three days in November 2008, gunmen attacked luxury hotels, a busy train station, a Jewish center, a café and other sites across India’s financial capital. By the time security forces ended the siege, more than 160 people had been killed and hundreds more wounded.

Behind the numbers were lives rooted in families, professions, faith and ordinary routines: a meal out, a business trip, a train journey, a night shift.

[CNN VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: “Remembering the victims of the Mumbai attacks”]

At the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, a landmark overlooking the Arabian Sea, guests and staff were trapped as gunfire and explosions echoed through corridors. Among those killed was Ashok Kapur, a prominent Indian banker and chairman of Yes Bank, whose death shook Mumbai’s financial community.

Kapur had helped build one of India’s fastest-growing private banks and was known among colleagues as a polished dealmaker. His killing underscored how the attacks reached into the heart of India’s business elite.

Also killed was British businessman Andreas Liveras, a Cyprus-born entrepreneur and founder of a luxury yacht company. He had reportedly spoken to journalists from inside the Taj before his death, describing the confusion and fear as guests sheltered amid the assault.

At the Oberoi-Trident hotel complex, another scene of prolonged violence, business travelers and tourists were caught in their rooms, restaurants and conference spaces. Some survived by barricading doors and switching off lights. Others did not make it out.

“This was not just an attack on buildings,” one Mumbai resident said in the days after the siege. “It was an attack on the idea of the city — on people from everywhere living and working together.”

[CNN VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: “Inside the siege at Mumbai’s luxury hotels”]

At Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, one of the world’s busiest train stations, gunmen fired into crowds of commuters. Many of the victims there were working people headed home or beginning overnight journeys — their names less widely known than those of executives and foreign visitors, but their losses no less profound.

Families searched hospitals and morgues for parents, siblings and children. Survivors later described stepping over luggage, broken glass and bodies as they tried to escape the station’s historic concourse.

The attacks also devastated Mumbai’s small Jewish community. At the Chabad-Lubavitch center known as Nariman House, Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg and his wife, Rivka, were killed along with other hostages. The young couple had moved to Mumbai to serve Jewish travelers and residents, running a center that offered prayer services, kosher meals and lodging.

Their toddler son, Moshe, survived after being carried to safety by his Indian nanny, Sandra Samuel, whose rescue became one of the most remembered stories of the attacks.

In the years since, Moshe’s survival has symbolized both the cruelty of the assault and the courage of those who risked their lives to save others.

[CNN VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: “The child rescued from Nariman House”]

Among the dead were also Americans Alan Scherr and his teenage daughter, Naomi, who had traveled to India as part of a spiritual retreat. They were killed at the Oberoi complex while dining. Friends described them as gentle, thoughtful and deeply committed to meditation and peace.

Their deaths resonated far beyond Mumbai, particularly among members of the spiritual community in Virginia where they had lived.

Other victims came from countries including Israel, the United States, Britain, Italy, Germany, Japan, Canada, Australia, Singapore and Thailand. But most of those killed were Indian — hotel employees, police officers, railway workers, drivers, security guards and ordinary citizens.

Several police officers died confronting the attackers, including Hemant Karkare, the chief of Mumbai’s Anti-Terrorism Squad; Ashok Kamte, a senior police officer; and Vijay Salaskar, a veteran encounter specialist. Their deaths became a defining part of India’s memory of the assault.

Indian officials later said the attackers had arrived by sea and were heavily armed, trained and guided as they moved through the city. The group Lashkar-e-Taiba, based in Pakistan, was blamed for carrying out the operation. The attacks sharply raised tensions between India and Pakistan and led to years of investigations, trials and diplomatic fallout.

But for families of the dead, the geopolitical consequences were secondary to the personal absences left behind.

A hotel worker who survived said staff members had stayed to help guests escape even as gunmen moved through the buildings. “They knew the passages, the kitchens, the stairways,” he said. “Many saved lives. Some lost their own.”

[CNN VIDEO PLACEHOLDER: “Hotel staff hailed as heroes after Mumbai attacks”]

Memorials in Mumbai now mark the places where the city was wounded: the bullet-scarred walls, the rebuilt hotel lobbies, the station platforms returned to their relentless rhythm. Each anniversary brings candles, flowers and photographs.

The victims were not united by nationality, wealth, religion or profession. They were united by chance — by being in Mumbai during a 60-hour assault that turned familiar places into killing grounds.

They were fathers and daughters. Tycoons and spiritualists. Police officers and cooks. Rabbis and commuters. Visitors and locals.

And in Mumbai, a city known for absorbing shock and moving forward, their names remain part of the story of a night when the world came under attack in one city — and never fully looked away.

# Identified victims of Mumbai siege include Americans, Jewish center emissaries and Indian police heroes

**November 2008 — CNN.com-style report**  
**MUMBAI, India** — As Indian authorities worked to identify the dead after the coordinated terror attacks across Mumbai, the names of victims began to reveal the international scope of the siege: American visitors, Jewish community workers, hotel guests and staff, and Indian police officers who died confronting the gunmen.

Among the Americans killed were **Alan Scherr, 58, and his daughter Naomi Scherr, 13**, of Virginia, who were in Mumbai as part of a meditation program with the Synchronicity Foundation, according to family representatives and associates. The father and daughter were killed at the **Oberoi-Trident hotel complex**, one of several sites targeted during the attacks.

Their family said the two had traveled to India seeking spiritual growth and community. Friends described Naomi as joyful and bright, and Alan Scherr as devoted to his family and spiritual practice.

Also among the dead were **Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg and his wife, Rivka Holtzberg**, emissaries of the **Chabad-Lubavitch** movement who ran the **Nariman House**, also known as the Chabad House, in Mumbai. The Jewish outreach center was seized by attackers during the siege.

The couple’s young son, **Moshe**, survived after being carried to safety by his nanny, an Indian woman who fled the building with the child. The deaths of the Holtzbergs drew mourning from Jewish communities worldwide and from Chabad leaders, who said the couple had dedicated their lives to serving Jewish residents and travelers in Mumbai.

Indian security forces and police also suffered heavy losses in the first hours of the attacks. Among the most prominent casualties were:

- **Hemant Karkare**, chief of Mumbai’s Anti-Terrorism Squad  
- **Ashok Kamte**, a senior Mumbai police official  
- **Vijay Salaskar**, a veteran police inspector known for his work against organized crime  
- **Tukaram Omble**, an assistant sub-inspector credited with helping capture one of the gunmen alive

Indian officials said the officers were killed while responding to the attacks, which struck luxury hotels, a railway station, a café, the Jewish center and other sites across the city.

The siege began late Wednesday, November 26, 2008, when gunmen opened fire and threw explosives at multiple locations in India’s financial capital. The attacks continued for nearly three days before Indian commandos ended the standoffs at the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident complex and Nariman House.

Authorities said the attackers arrived by sea and used automatic weapons and grenades. India later blamed the Pakistan-based militant group **Lashkar-e-Taiba** for the assault. Pakistan denied official involvement but acknowledged that some suspects were linked to Pakistani territory.

The final death toll exceeded 160, with hundreds more wounded. Victims came from India and numerous other countries, including the United States, Israel and several European nations.

Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh condemned the attacks as an assault on India’s sovereignty and vowed to pursue those responsible. Around Mumbai, residents held vigils for the dead, while families waited outside hospitals and morgues for confirmation of missing loved ones.

The Scherr family, the Holtzbergs and the fallen Indian officers became some of the most widely recognized names among the victims — symbols of the civilians and first responders caught in one of India’s deadliest terrorist attacks.

**CNN contributors in Mumbai, New Delhi, London and Atlanta contributed to this report.**
